newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM sees rise in foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM sees rise in foreign investment.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said on Tuesday he expected a strong increase in foreign investment over the next two years as the country's privatisation process draws to a close.

Addressing a conference attended by foreign businessmen, Drnovsek said the first round of privatisation was based on management and employee buy-outs, while the second stage should include the search for domestic and foreign equity partners.

"The second round of privatisation starting now will probably result in a significant increase of foreign investments," the prime minister told representatives of foreign companies at the meeting organised by The Economist.

While Slovenia has made strides in privatising state-owned concerns since it declared independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991, many foreign firms believe Drnovsek's centrist coalition government could do a lot more.
"There is an inbalance between what Western companies want and what the government is offering," Daniel Thorniley, senior vice president of the Economist conference told Reuters.
He said investors were looking for more liberal foreign investment legislation coupled with greater liberalisation of cross-border financial transactions and the banking sector.

Slovenia currently permits foreigners to own only a minority share in most companies, while foreign banks can establish their subsidiaries in Slovenia only after laying out a substantial amount of capital.
At the same time, cross-border transfers are burdened by complicated bureaucratic procedures and red tape.

"Although Slovenia offers a relatively stable and predictable investment environment, investors are looking for additional encouragement like tax deductions and employment incentives," said Les Boonney, managing director of the East and Central European branch of the California-based software producer Oracle.
Foreign direct investments in 1995 rose to around $150 million from $83.7 million a year earlier and represented 0.8 percent of Slovenia's GDP.
But foreign businessmen said privatisation was only likely to have any effect on greater investments by the beginning of next year at the earliest.
Drnovsek's government faces a general election on November 10 and the formation of a coalition could take weeks.
"I expect it will take another 18 months before foreign investments start to rise on the basis of privatisation," Thorniley said.
Around 700 Slovenian companies have been fully privatised so far, while a further 1,266 are still in the process. Those should be completed by the end of 1997.
